clue.text: Aggressiveness of French betrothed

parts.note: de is the French word for 'of'
a fiancé is a man engaged to be married

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's engaged partner turns out to have a combative streak.
explanation.definitionFit: Defiance is bold, challenging resistance, an openly hostile and confrontational attitude.

clue.text: Shopkeeper makes a return about a bearded one

indicators.note: returning means the following pieces are read backwards

parts.note: re means about, concerning
the pard, an old word for leopard, as in Shakespeare's soldier 'bearded like the pard'

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper heads back towards a man with a beard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes a return' reverses RE + PARD to give DRAPER; the pard is the leopard of 'All the world's a stage'.
explanation.definitionFit: A draper is a retailer selling cloth and fabrics, a kind of shopkeeper.

clue.text: A healing creed by a foreign priest

parts.note: a faith is a religious belief, a creed
a curé is a French parish priest

explanation.surface: A religious belief brought by a priest from abroad that cures the sick.
explanation.definitionFit: A faith cure is a recovery from illness brought about by prayer and belief rather than medicine.

clue.text: Nigel badly needs Bill around to be of such good behaviour

indicators.note: the bill letters go round the outside of the jumbled name

parts.note: AC, short for account, which is a bill

indicators.note: the name is written badly, its letters out of order

explanation.surface: A badly behaved Nigel needs a bill wrapped round him to behave like a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' is not a man's name beside Nigel but an account, abbreviated in the usual way; 'needs' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Angelic describes conduct as sweet and virtuous as that of an angel.

clue.text: Shepherd comes right into a bit of money

indicators.note: the letter for right goes inside the word for a piece of money

parts.note: a coin is a small piece of money

explanation.surface: A shepherd comes into a bit of cash, rightly.
explanation.walkthrough: Corin is the old shepherd in Shakespeare's As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: Corin is the shepherd character in As You Like It, a name from pastoral tradition.

clue.text: Property of the fool at the outset

clue.text: With science, what he writes causes religious divisions

parts.note: SC is an abbreviation for science
his MS, his manuscript, is what he writes

explanation.surface: Combining science with his writings causes splits in the church.
explanation.walkthrough: MS is the standard abbreviation for manuscript, so what he writes is 'his MS'.
explanation.definitionFit: Schisms are splits within a religious body into opposing factions.

clue.text: Like Omar's final glass

parts.note: the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam ends with the request to 'turn down' a glass with nothing in it

explanation.walkthrough: FitzGerald's Rubaiyat closes: 'turn down an empty Glass!'
explanation.definitionFit: The last quatrain asks that the cup be upturned, drained of wine, in memory of the poet.

clue.text: This kind of committee for drivers ?

definitions.text: This kind of committee for drivers ?

parts.words: This kind of committee for drivers ?
parts.note: a committee that guides a project's direction, imagined as one that handles cars

explanation.definitionFit: A steering committee sets the agenda of a body, while steering is what drivers do with the wheel.

clue.text: Tell-tale footwear ?

parts.note: soft shoes worn to creep quietly, imagined as shoes that tell tales, as a sneak does

explanation.definitionFit: Sneakers are soft-soled shoes, and a sneak is a tell-tale who informs on others.

clue.text: Horner's participation ? Not exactly

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Little Jack Horner put his thumb, not quite the other digit named in the phrase, into his Christmas pie

explanation.walkthrough: Little Jack Horner 'put in his thumb and pulled out a plum'; 'Not exactly' admits the idiom names a different digit.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a part or interest in some affair is the idiomatic meaning, here tied to the rhyme's pastry.

clue.text: Argentine revolutionary in lone sort of formation

indicators.note: the revolutionary's name is placed inside the rearranged letters of the next word
sort is read as a verb, so the letters of lone are sorted into a new order

parts.note: Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: Guevara stands alone in some odd military arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Argentine revolutionary' is Che Guevara, whose short name crosswords use constantly; 'sort of' looks like vague padding before 'formation' but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An echelon is a stepped arrangement of troops, ships or aircraft, a type of formation.

clue.text: Like the' Speaker, who applies the test '

parts.note: as means like, in the same manner
a sayer is one who says something, a speaker

explanation.surface: Someone who, like the Commons Speaker, puts things to the test.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Speaker' suggests the chair of the House of Commons, but it is just someone who speaks.
explanation.definitionFit: An assayer analyses metals and ores, testing them for purity.

clue.text: Broken hutch Momma Rabbit gets out of — for weed-killer?

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, so its letters are put back together differently

parts.note: a doe is a female rabbit

explanation.surface: A mother rabbit escapes from a damaged hutch, looking for something to kill weeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' rearranges HUTCH plus DOE (the mother rabbit), with 'gets out of' joining it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dutch hoe is a push hoe with a flat blade for slicing through weeds, a tool for killing them.

clue.text: Falsely spy on his sleepy State

indicators.note: the letters are falsely arranged, so must be put in their true order

explanation.surface: A secret agent wrongly watching him in a drowsy country.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'State' suggests a nation, but it is just a condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypnosis is a trance-like condition resembling sleep.

clue.text: Singer somehow lost key

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Singer somehow lost key (5)' for SIREN: 'Singer' defines it, but no word or anagram of 'lost key' gives SIREN; the scan prints the same words.

clue.text: Let it rip? One takes on this performance.

parts.note: rend it, tear it apart
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Go for it! Someone takes on this show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let it rip?' is not 'go all out' but an instruction to tear it: REND IT. 'takes' joins I to ON.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendition is an interpretation or performance of a song, role or piece of music.

clue.text: Resisting work — the work of a model

parts.note: op, short for opus, a work
posing for an artist or camera is what a model does

explanation.surface: Fighting against work, the sort a model does.
explanation.definitionFit: Opposing means setting oneself against something, standing in resistance to it.

clue.text: Part of the triple attack that makes us fold

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A piece of a three-pronged assault that forces us to give in.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleat is a fold sewn into fabric, the thing that gives cloth its creases.

clue.text: Bids for harbour craft

definitions.meaning: formal offers to supply goods or do work at a price
small boats ferrying supplies or people between ship and shore

explanation.surface: Offers made for boats in the port.
explanation.definitionFit: A tender is both a formal offer of a price and a small vessel serving a larger ship.

clue.text: Letters before the sixteenth one has to 'put off

parts.note: post is the letters delivered by the mail
the sixteenth letter of the alphabet is P

explanation.surface: Some letters come before the sixteenth, which has to be delayed.
explanation.definitionFit: To postpone is to defer or delay something until a later time.

clue.text: Chairman and arbiter shortly returning to curtail 19

indicators.note: to curtail is to cut short, so the chairman's title loses its tail

parts.note: a professor holds a university chair

indicators.note: returning means the shortened official is read backwards

parts.note: ref, short for referee

explanation.surface: The head of a meeting and an umpire turn back to cut short the bids.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 refers to TENDERS, here as a verb. A chairman is a professor, who holds a chair; 'to curtail' cuts that to PROF. 'returning' turns REF into FER.
explanation.definitionFit: To proffer is to hold out or offer, the verb sense of tender.

clue.text: Principles observed by East when under canvas

indicators.note: under canvas means within the tents, so the letter goes inside the word

parts.note: tents are made of canvas

explanation.surface: Beliefs kept by someone from the east while camping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when under canvas' puts E inside TENTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenets are doctrines or beliefs held as true, the principles of a creed.

clue.text: Gibbons' made music in Arden

definitions.meaning: first name of the Jacobean composer Gibbons
the lover who carves verses on trees in Shakespeare's forest comedy

explanation.surface: The composer Gibbons playing in the Forest of Arden.
explanation.walkthrough: Arden is the forest where As You Like It is set.
explanation.definitionFit: Orlando Gibbons was an English composer, and Orlando is the young hero of Shakespeare's As You Like It, set in the Forest of Arden.

clue.text: The king is dead.! So afterwards ?

parts.note: late describes someone who has died
R, for Rex, Latin king

explanation.surface: The monarch has died, so what comes next?
explanation.walkthrough: 'The king is dead' is the start of the royal proclamation, read here as R is LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Later means at a subsequent time, coming after.

clue.text: My word!

parts.note: read not as an exclamation of surprise but as a pledge: giving someone my word

explanation.definitionFit: A promise is an assurance given on one's honour that something will be done.

clue.text: Ripe Indian kind of sahib :

definitions.meaning: Anglo-Indian for ripe or cooked, from Hindi
a proper gentleman in Raj slang

explanation.surface: A mature Indian, a genuine sort of gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Pukka is Hindi for ripe or cooked and came to mean genuine; a pukka sahib was a true gentleman in British India.

clue.text: Where convicts are held at the last possible moment ?

definitions.meaning: inside the 'nick', British slang for prison, doing time
only just in time, at the critical instant

explanation.surface: Prisoners are kept locked up until the final moment.
explanation.walkthrough: NICK is British slang for prison and TIME is a sentence served there, so a convict is both in the nick and doing time.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means just before it would be too late, while the literal reading puts someone in jail serving a sentence.

clue.text: Hag is right, maybe, to be so showy

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: An old woman might be correct to dress so flamboyantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Garish means gaudy, too bright and flashy in colour or style.

clue.text: Presents Johnny took so long buying ?

parts.note: the old song 'Oh dear, what can the matter be? Johnny's so long at the fair', where he promised to buy ribbons

explanation.surface: Gifts that took Johnny ages to purchase.
explanation.walkthrough: The folk song has Johnny 'so long at the fair' buying blue ribbons, and a gift bought at a fair is a fairing.
explanation.definitionFit: Fairings are small gifts or souvenirs bought at a fair to take home.
